{
  "analysis": "The primary failures stem from the 'GmbH Company Names' rule being too greedy (capturing preceding context like 'Partei' or 'der') and the 'BFG and VwGH Acronyms' rule failing to capture multi-word city names after 'Landesgerichts' (e.g., 'St. Pölten', 'Wien') and missing specific court names like 'Oberlandesgerichts Linz'.   "strategy": "1. Replace the greedy 'GmbH Company Names' rule with a strict pattern that requires a proper noun prefix and stops before 'GmbH' or 'GmbH & Co KG'. 2. Replace the 'BFG and VwGH Acronyms' rule with a comprehensive court name pattern that explicitly handles 'Landesgerichts' + City, 'Oberlandesgerichts' + City, and 'Bezirksgerichts' + City, including genitive forms. 3. Add specific rules for 'OG' law firms and 'GmbH & Co KG' entities. 4. Add a rule for 'Obersten Gerichtshofs' (genitive). 5. Delete the old 'BFG and VwGH Acronyms' and 'GmbH Company Names' rules to prevent conflicts.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "GmbH Company Names",
      "description": "Matches company names ending in 'GmbH' with a required proper noun prefix, strictly excluding preceding context like 'der' or 'Partei'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 18,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "(?<![a-zäöüß])\\b([A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&]+)*\\s+GmbH)\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "GmbH & Co KG Company Names",
      "description": "Matches company names ending in 'GmbH & Co KG' with a proper noun prefix, ensuring the full legal form is captured.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 19,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "(?<![a-zäöüß])\\b([A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&]+)*\\s+GmbH\\s+&\\s+Co\\s+KG)\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "Law Firm OG Names",
      "description": "Matches law firm names ending in 'Rechtsanwälte OG' or 'Rechtsanwälte-Partnerschaft', handling complex names with '&' and 'u'.",

      "priority": 17,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "\\b([A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&\\.]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][A-Za-zäöüß\\-\\d\\s&\\.]+)*\\s+(?:Rechtsanwälte\\s+OG|Rechtsanwälte\\-Partnerschaft))\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "Specific Court Names Genitive",
      "description": "Matches genitive forms of courts like 'Obersten Gerichtshofs', 'Landesgerichts', 'Bezirksgerichts' followed by city names.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 20,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "\\b(?:Obersten\\s+Gerichtshofs|Landesgerichts\\s+(?:für\\s+Zivilrechtssachen\\s+Wien|für\\s+Strafsachen\\s+Wien|St\\.\\s+Pölten|Wels|Linz|Salzburg|Graz|Feldkirch|Leoben|Wien)|Oberlandesgerichts\\s+(?:Linz|Wien|Graz)|Bezirksgerichts\\s+Purkersdorf)\\b"

      "name": "Landesgericht City Pattern",
      "description": "Matches 'Landesgericht' or 'Landesgerichts' followed by a city name, capturing the full entity including genitive endings.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 19,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "\\b(Landesgerichts?\\s+(?:für\\s+Zivilrechtssachen\\s+Wien|für\\s+Strafsachen\\s+Wien|St\\.\\s+Pölten|Wels|Linz|Salzburg|Graz|Feldkirch|Leoben|Wien))\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "Oberlandesgericht City Pattern",

      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 19,

        "text": "$1",

        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "\\b(Oberlandesgerichts?\\s+(?:Linz|Wien|Graz))\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "Oberster Gerichtshof Genitive",
      "description": "Matches 'Obersten Gerichtshofs' (genitive) which was previously missed.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 20,
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "content": "\\bObersten\\s+Gerichtshofs\\b"
    },
    {
      "name": "VwGH Acronym",
      "description": "Matches the VwGH (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) acronym.",
      "format": "regex",
      "priority": 15,
      "output_template": {

        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority
